analysis.one_liner: Puts a small tax on Wall Street trades to fund jobs, health, infrastructure, and climate programs, rebating it for lower-income households.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on May 22, 2019 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The Inclusive Prosperity Act would place a 0.5% tax on every purchase of stock, 0.1% on bonds, and 0.005% on derivatives traded or cleared in the United States, or involving a US party. The tax is collected by exchanges and brokers, so individual investors pay it as a small add-on to trade costs. Revenue would go toward free college, expanded health care, housing, infrastructure, and climate programs, and households earning under $50,000 ($75,000 married) would get a credit rebating any tax they paid.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary working people stand to gain the most if the programs in the bill's findings section were funded: free college and student debt relief, expanded Medicare and Medicaid, housing assistance, job training, public infrastructure, and clean-energy investments. Lower- and middle-income households who do trade stocks (for example, small individual investors) would be made whole through the tax credit. The high costs fall on high-volume traders: the bill's findings state that high-frequency trading may account for as much as 70% of the market, and those firms would pay the tax on most of their volume.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Working families funded by new Wall Street tax revenue

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 0.5% tax on stock purchases, 0.1% on bonds, and 0.005% on derivatives, generating revenue the bill's stated purposes direct toward free college, expanded Medicare and Medicaid, housing assistance, infrastructure, and climate programs.
Rebates the entire tax to households earning under $50,000 ($75,000 married filing jointly), so the lowest-income traders — including many retirement savers — would pay nothing out of pocket.

The bill's findings argue a transaction tax would curb high-frequency trading, which it says may be as much as 70% of the market and contributes to price volatility, while having a negligible impact on the average investor.
The tax applies broadly to trades involving any US person, including trades executed abroad, with anti-avoidance rules directing Treasury to prevent use of non-US parties to escape the tax.

analysis.who_pays: Wall Street trading firms, banks, hedge funds, and other large institutional investors who trade in enormous volume would bear most of the cost. Some of the tax would likely be passed through to ordinary investors as slightly higher trading costs, mutual fund fees, and marginally lower investment returns — the bill's credit does not fully cover households above the income threshold, and indirect costs through retirement funds are not rebated at all. Exchanges and brokers would also carry the administrative burden of collecting and remitting the tax on every covered trade.
analysis.who_pays_short: High-volume traders and large investment firms

drawbacks.text: The tax applies to every purchase of stock, bonds, and derivatives, and the cost can be passed through to small investors and retirement savers; only direct payments by households under $50,000 are rebated, while indirect costs through mutual funds and 401(k)s are not.

The bill exempts the initial issuance of securities, tax-exempt municipal bonds, short-term debt, and securities lending arrangements, narrowing what the tax covers and leaving the amount of revenue actually raised uncertain relative to the ambitious program list in its findings.
An added cost on every US securities trade gives some trading activity an incentive to move to overseas venues, which could erode the revenue and cost US financial centers some trading business.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax is deliberately small (a half-percent on stocks) and the full rebate for households under $50,000 insulates most of the people the bill aims to help. The honest objections are that some cost leaks onto ordinary retirement savers through fund-level trades, and that the bill commits the revenue to a long aspirational list of programs without an actual appropriations mechanism. On balance the design is workable; the bill's problem was never its drafting — it was that it never received a single committee action.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — ever happened before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Sen. Sanders introduced the Inclusive Prosperity Act of 2019 in the Senate on May 22, 2019, with Sen. Gillibrand as its cosponsor.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
The Finance Committee took no further action: no hearing, no markup, and no vote are recorded for the bill for the rest of the 116th Congress.
The bill never came to the Senate floor, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 without the bill ever advancing past committee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-volume Wall Street trading firms, hedge funds, and large asset managers are better off: the 0.5% stock tax, 0.1% bond tax, and 0.005% derivative tax were never imposed, and the programs the revenue would have funded — college, health care, housing, infrastructure, climate — received no funding from it either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wall Street trading firms that avoided the tax

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Inclusive Prosperity Act of 2019, proposing a 0.5% tax on stock trades and smaller taxes on bonds and derivatives to fund social and infrastructure programs.

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — the only cosponsor it attracted in the Senate.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup for the bill after it was referred to the Finance Committee on May 22, 2019.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote during the 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was confined to one Independent and one Democrat — two of 100 senators — and no Republican signed on; with Republicans holding the Senate and its committee chairs, the bill had no path to action.

industries.industry: Securities trading firms and high-frequency traders
industries.note: A 0.5% tax on every stock purchase, 0.1% on bonds, and 0.005% on derivatives would fall heaviest on firms trading in massive volume; the bill's own findings argue high-frequency trading is up to 70% of the market and destabilizes prices. Blocking the bill preserved their cost structure.

These firms would be required to collect and remit the tax on every covered trade, adding compliance costs, while lower trading volume would cut commission and fee revenue. Killing the bill spared them both.

industries.industry: Large asset managers and wealthy institutional investors
industries.note: Institutional funds and wealthy investors exceed the bill's $50,000/$75,000 rebate threshold and would absorb the tax on their trades with no offset. They benefited from the bill's inaction.
Tax-exempt municipal bonds are expressly excluded from the tax, leaving them untaxed relative to other fixed-income securities — a carve-out that survived because the bill never advanced.
